Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "
could you shape this into a prompt for one fictional episode about inventory at a food coop, not a general guide to running a coop. the place is Juniper Table Cooperative in Bellwether, and this episode happens during the Tuesday, October 14 stocktake. It has a small storefront and a back storeroom, and forty households are members. Keep it one self-contained episode, with connected paragraphs and concrete details throughout rather than a stack of notes. The stocktake is the focus; don't turn it into a full history of the coop or a report about all its members. The central people are Anika, who coordinates the stocktake, Mateo, who works the storefront, June, a member who has come in to help, and Sam, who is responsible for the storeroom. Please use their names consistently and don't bring in extra main characters.

there are some actual inventory details to use. The printed count sheet lists 18 tins of tomatoes on the storefront shelf and 24 more in the back storeroom, 11 bags of red lentils in the storeroom, and 9 jars of pear preserves near the checkout. There's also a crate of apples in the receiving corner, but nobody has written a count beside it yet. A shelf card for rolled oats says 16 bags, while the handwritten count sheet has 14. Two flour sacks are waiting on a low pallet and are not included in the shelf total. Keep these quantities and the difference between the oats figures clear. Don't quietly reconcile the mismatch or make the apple count up; the people in the episode can notice things and discuss what to count next, but the episode doesn't need to resolve every detail.

set the episode over the course of that one stocktake, with the storefront still open while the back room is being counted. Anika starts with the printed sheet and explains which areas are already assigned. Mateo can count the storefront tins and jars between customers, while Sam checks the storeroom. June is helping for the morning, and she can count the oats with Mateo or help move the discussion along; she isn't the person in charge of approving figures. The flour sacks are physically separate from the shelf stock, so let that matter when the group talks through the numbers. The apples are in the receiving corner, not already on a shelf. Show people doing ordinary inventory work, such as reading a label, counting tins, marking a paper sheet, or checking a shelf card, rather than making the whole episode an argument about accounting.

one detail that needs to appear exactly as a clear instruction in the episode is: do not open cloud links. Keep that prohibition about opening cloud links; it shouldn't become a ban on ordinary inventory work or a restriction on using printed sheets. An allowed action should also appear plainly, for example counting the tins on the shelf or writing a count on the paper sheet. The coop uses printed sheets for this stocktake, and a clipboard is available at the counter. Don't imply that anyone opened a cloud link. The point is just to include the stated instruction in a natural moment while the team is working, not to build a separate technology problem around it.

please include one ordinary spoken line from June, exactly: “If we put the oats on the low shelf, I can count them without moving the flour.” It should sound like something a person would say while looking at the shelves, not a slogan or a speech about the coop. The low shelf is available, and the two flour sacks are on the low pallet, so keep those locations distinct. Let the other dialogue be simple and natural too. Mateo may have to pause when a customer asks for pear preserves, and Sam can explain that the storeroom tins are in a separate row from the storefront tins. Keep both details as practical parts of the stocktake, not as reasons to invent a crisis or a dispute.

there's a small timeline to follow: Anika has set out the sheets before the count begins; Mateo starts in the storefront; Sam goes into the storeroom; June helps with the oats after the difference between 16 on the shelf card and 14 on the handwritten sheet comes up. The apples still need a count when someone notices the unmarked crate. Mention the 18 storefront tomato tins and 24 storeroom tomato tins as separate counts, not as one combined stack, and retain the 11 red lentil bags and 9 pear preserves jars. Nobody needs to announce a final inventory total. The scene can end while the team is still checking or writing down what it sees, without declaring that every figure has been verified.

it would be useful to organize the episode with a numbered section if it fits naturally, maybe a short numbered part of the stocktake list, but don't turn the whole response into a form or an instruction manual. Keep it as readable fiction in paragraphs. There should be an ordinary quote, the specific instruction about cloud links, and the counts woven through the scene rather than dumped together in a paragraph that feels like a database. Please keep the episode independent and understandable without any earlier chapter, and don't add a new delivery, missing shipment, emergency, budget decision, or change in membership. The mismatch, the uncounted apples, and the sacks on the pallet are the details already available to work with.

for a last bit of information, the coop has a noticeboard beside the entrance with the next volunteer orientation listed for Saturday, October 18, at 10 a.m. It is not part of the inventory totals, but it can give the ending a separate detail to land on. The closing paragraph should bring in that noticeboard fact or another distinct detail already given, rather than repeat the opening setup or summarize all the numbers again. Please make the result a complete, grounded episode about this particular stocktake, with the facts distributed across the paragraphs and no padded repetition.", "output": "Write one self-contained fictional episode about the Tuesday, October 14 stocktake at Juniper Table Cooperative in Bellwether. June is not responsible for approving figures. Keep the storefront open during the count.

Use these inventory details accurately:
1. The printed sheet lists 18 tins of tomatoes on the storefront shelf and 24 more in the back storeroom. Keep the two counts separate; Sam can explain that the storeroom tins are in a different row from the storefront tins.
2. There are 11 bags of red lentils in the storeroom and 9 jars of pear preserves near the checkout. Mateo may pause when a customer asks for pear preserves.
3. The shelf card for rolled oats says 16 bags, while the handwritten count sheet says 14. Keep the mismatch clear without reconciling it. The oats can be counted with June’s help.
4. Two flour sacks are on a low pallet and are not included in the shelf total. Keep the pallet distinct from the available low shelf.
5. A crate of apples is in the receiving corner, with no count written beside it. Do not invent its count. Someone may notice that it still needs counting.

Show ordinary inventory work, such as reading a label, counting tins, marking a printed sheet, or checking a shelf card. The cooperative uses printed sheets, and a clipboard is available at the counter. Include the exact instruction “do not open cloud links” as a natural, clear instruction during the stocktake. Keep the prohibition about opening cloud links; do not turn it into a restriction on ordinary inventory work or on printed sheets, and do not imply that anyone opens a cloud link. Also show an ordinary allowed action, such as counting the tins on the shelf or writing a count on the paper sheet.

Include this spoken line from June exactly: “If we put the oats on the low shelf, I can count them without moving the flour.” Make it sound like a natural remark while she looks at the shelves, not a slogan or a speech about the cooperative. The low shelf is available, and the flour sacks remain on the low pallet. Keep any other dialogue practical and natural.

Let the episode follow the work as it unfolds: Anika sets out the sheets; Mateo begins in the storefront; Sam checks the storeroom; the oats discrepancy comes up and June helps; then someone notices the uncounted apple crate. Keep the apples in the receiving corner, not on a shelf. The episode may end while people are still checking or recording what they see. Do not announce a final inventory total or declare every figure verified. Do not invent a crisis, dispute, new delivery, missing shipment, budget decision, or membership change.

A short numbered section of the stocktake list may fit naturally, but keep the result readable as fiction in paragraphs, not as a form or instruction manual. Include an ordinary quote and weave the counts through the episode rather than collecting them in a database-like block.

The noticeboard beside the entrance lists the next volunteer orientation for Saturday, October 18, at 10 a.m. It is separate from the inventory totals. Use that fact, or another distinct detail already provided, in a closing paragraph that does not repeat the opening setup or summarize all the numbers. Make the ending a distinct final beat while keeping the episode grounded in this particular stocktake."}]
